https://www.dw.com/en/ratko-mladic-the-m.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JWvb Ratko Mladic, seen here in April 1993, was later found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes committed during the Bosnian war Image: Chris Helgren/REUTERS Advertisement More than 30 years after the end of the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic , the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army. Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later. At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II . The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children. Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the three-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country half of its total population at the time. Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 'Butcher of the Balkans' In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague. International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans." He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian war. Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy. "Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying. Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Career in the Yugoslav army At the beginning of the Croatian war in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence. Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic. Mladic (left) and Radovan Karadzic, the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs during the war (seen here in August 1993), were both convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia Image: picture-alliance/ dpa Flight, arrest and final verdict At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just 2 years old when his father, a Partisan follower of Yugoslavia's longtime communist leader Josip Broz Titos, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview. As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class and quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state. Serbian nationalist Before the end of the Bosnian war in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure. The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian war. Ratko Mladic life sentence upheld To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video War criminal who saw himself as a hero Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. UN officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long overdue, but an important acknowledgment of their suffering. Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic." Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls. While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding, and later survived several strokes while in prison. Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84. This article was originally written in German. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ev.text: Figure caption, Watch: Emergency services at the scene of shooting near Paris By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Â and Â Jacob Phillips Published 23 October 2026, 12:09 BST Updated 1 hour ago French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack". Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there has ever been a random racial killing like this. The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La VerriÃ¨re - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested. Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition. Visiting the scene of the attack in Trappes, Macron said people had been targeted for their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root". The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise". The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions which had been "automatically expunged". The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV. A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added. The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning. The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said. The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La VerriÃ¨re. A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La VerriÃ¨re on the main N10 road that runs through the town. Image source, EPA Image caption, French police inspect the scene of the shooting in Trappes, near Paris Image source, Getty Images Image caption, French firefighters and police were seen at a petrol station in the area The mother of the injured 12-year-old told French broadcaster RTL her daughter suffered eight gunshot wounds and needed surgery. "How could anyone do this to a child?" she asked. The mother said her daughter had been wearing a headscarf and questioned whether this was why she was attacked. "She's a child who was born in France, in Trappes. She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France," she added. The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window. A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two. PNAT said its investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts. The anti-terrorist office also said its investigation is looking into "conspiracy with a terrorist group for the purpose of preparing crimes against persons". https://www.dw.com/en/french-officials-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PGaU Prefer DW on Google Stores in several countries across Europe recently experienced fridge and freezer issues Image: Elsa Rancel/Ouest-France/PHOTOPQR/MAXPPP/IMAGO Advertisement French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the attacks on French supermarkets last month came from Iran, and were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) , the elite branch of Iran's armed forces that answers directly to its religious leadership. "This attack is unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," Barrot said, adding "we will implement sanctions at the European level against all those responsible for this attack." What happened during the alleged refrigeration cyberattack? While the cyberattack was comparatively simple, it nevertheless had serious consequences for hundreds of supermarkets, spoiling large quantities of produce and in some cases setting temperatures so high that refrigeration units caught fire. It was launched overnight on October 11-12, affecting around 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets. The hack forced supermarkets to pull multiple products from their cold storage displays, and to throw many of them away entirely Image: Fred Tanneau/AFP A series of similar incidents also affected French supermarkets last week , and authorities even reported a failed attempt to hack cooling units at blood banks . Supermarkets in other European countries have reported similar security breaches, as have US authorities. It was not clear if any of all of these instances were connected. What did French prosecutors say about the case? Meanwhile, a Paris prosecutor provided details on the hacking probe: "A judicial investigation has been opened against the head of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, against his two deputies, and against any other individuals who may be identified," Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said. Barrot's Foreign Ministry said that France "condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran." Photograph: FBI View image in fullscreen Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, pictured here in FBI custody in May, has been accused by US federal prosecutors of plotting a foiled attack on the RAF Fairford base in September. Photograph: FBI UK news US prosecutors charge Iranian operative allegedly responsible for UK air force base attack New indictment claims Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in US custody Andrew Roth in Washington Tue 10 Nov 2026 16.57 EST Last modified on Tue 10 Nov 2026 19.03 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US federal prosecutors have said that an Iranian operative jailed in New York was responsible for the foiled attack on a UK air force base where American B-1 bombers were stationed. A new indictment alleged that Mohammad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian and Iraqi national, plotted while in custody and then transmitted plans – using coded messages in calls to his family – to two co-conspirators to buy large quantities of chemicals that could be used as explosives in an attack on the RAF Fairford base in September. Al-Saadi, who was accused of being associated with Kata’ib Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, was said to have planned the attack as retribution for the US war in Iran. He had already been charged for his alleged links to 18 terrorist attacks in Europe and for allegedly planning to bomb a synagogue in New York as well, according to a statement by the southern district of New York. He was already imprisoned when he began planning the attack, according to the indictment, which said he then transmitted his plans by using coded messages in calls to his family to pass on to Mohsen Mohajeri, an operative of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and another Iranian, Mohammad Ali al-Hassani. Al-Hassani then tasked others with surveilling the Fairford RAF base and with procuring vans and barrels of fuel, and researching the purchase of chemical accelerants and metallic objects to be used as shrapnel, the indictment claimed. Five men from London were arrested in the village of Whelford, near RAF Fairford, on 27 September on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences, after a farmer reported vans blocking a road near the base while on her way back from a party. RAF Fairford is the European home for US air force bombers and was used by the US during its bombing campaign against Iran. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued a statement noting RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers and saying any bases used by the US to attack Iran, including Fairford, were “legitimate targets” . “As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said the US attorney Jamie McDonald. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas.” “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical – it is very real,” he added. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/13/euro.text: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland this week following a visit to the Kremlin, after which they pushed for Europeans to be present at the negotiating table in future talks.The pair landed at a military base near Dublin on Thursday, where they addressed the media alongside Zelenskyy.Other matters, such as a ceasefire - or any concrete steps towards ending the war - took a back seat as the key point of progress announced by the trio was that European negotiators would be involved in future discussions on ending Russia's all-out war on Ukraine.Zelenskyy told reporters that Europe would have a "voice" during future talks and that it would not be kept "separately" on the sidelines - as had happened in recent trilateral negotiations between US, Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi."This is important for us because the war is in Europe. We will be member of EU in the future and that's why it's very important. For prosperity and for security guarantees it's very important to have Europe," Zelenskyy said.In a post on X, Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, added: "Both sides have now agreed to expand the next round of negotiations to include our European partners.""This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia," he wrote.Moscow has not confirmed whether it has agreed to include European negotiators in subsequent talks.In comments shared by the Russian foreign ministry on Friday morning, presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said: "For our part, the position of the Europeans has been comprehensively outlined. They are striving by every means possible to join the negotiations, but, as our President has said, they must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war."It comes after Witkoff and Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier this week.During their meeting, Putin signalled that Russia would not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country, dampening hopes of a nearing deal to end the war.
